metric.why: A hall can be full by power and half empty by space, or the reverse. Tracking both per cabinet is how operators find capacity they already own before building more.
metric.metric: Stranded power and space per cabinet
metric.definition: Utility power or floor space that is allocated and paid for but cannot be used, because the other of the pair ran out first or airflow limits were reached.

reading.body:
Data center operators cannot fully use power or floor space in most cabinets, because one constraint fills before the other, creating stranded capacity they already pay for.

A cabinet represents a discrete unit where power delivery, physical space, and airflow form a closed system. When any one of these three hits its limit first, the remaining two cannot be used even though they are provisioned and paid for. An operator might have allocated sufficient kilowatts but insufficient floor area for the servers that would consume them, or vice versa. Airflow constraints, which depend on the geometry of equipment and cooling infrastructure, can make either power or space unusable before its nominal limit is reached.

For AI deployment, stranded capacity matters because it determines the actual density at which compute can be deployed. Theoretical power budgets and floor space mean nothing without the ability to use both simultaneously. This gap between allocated resources and usable resources directly affects how much incremental compute a data center can add without new construction. It also reveals whether a facility was designed for balanced growth or whether prior build decisions created mismatches now difficult to correct.

This metric does not measure total data center capacity, the cost of stranded resources, or which constraint is most often binding across the industry. It does not track whether stranded capacity is temporary or permanent, or whether operators can reconfigure cabinets to reduce it.
